live_attach.answer_text:
Jesus was our one Mediator, truly God and truly man, the whole center our life turned on. Every household under our catechism said it the same way, each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; on the third day he rose again from the dead, and just as he is risen from death, he lives and reigns forever. That confession is what we have. We do not argue it out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.

What he did for us, we say just as plainly. He redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver; it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. He is my Lord - each of us says it - I am his very own, to live under him in his kingdom and serve him in eternal righteousness, innocence, and blessedness.

And he is present, still, where we gather. At the table, his true body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine - food for our daily struggle, not a memorial only. In the Word preached and sung in our own language, so ordinary people who cannot read Latin can learn it. In the promise spoken to the ears - the absolution given as though from God himself, the "given for you" that makes a frightened conscience sure. We battle not against flesh and blood but against the devil himself, and the Word of Christ is our one weapon in that fight.

We do not reach Jesus by climbing toward a higher, more perfect life the way monks once claimed to. We reach him by trust in the promise, held in the ordinary callings God gives us - father, mother, ruler, or preacher - none holier than another. A father teaching his household the three parts, morning and night, is doing the same holy work a pastor does at the pulpit. Jesus, for us, is not somewhere else, reached by leaving the world. He is the Word that reached us where we were, and the presence that feeds us at the table we return to, over and over, for life.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

live_attach.answer_text:
What connected us to Jesus was the Word — his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench — buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

By what path did it arrive? Through the whole chain of teaching and handing down that Scripture names for itself — Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful people, faithful people to others still. We do not trace an unbroken chain of witnesses, hand laid on hand, from the apostles' own day to ours. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we hold instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. That Word was preached, printed in our own language, sung in hymns the unlearned could memorize, and taught at every household table where a father examined his children on the three parts. The path is not one we walked ourselves across fifteen centuries. It is the path the Word itself took, from mouth to ear, from print to eye, from the catechism's own question — what does this mean — to the answer a child gives back.

live_attach.answer_text:
We would say this: the inability itself is exactly what we expected, and it is not the thing that damns you.

Believing, for us, is not a work you perform to meet a requirement. It is trust given by the Holy Spirit through the Word, where the Word is spoken and heard. You cannot produce it on your own, the way you produce sweat by running or heat by striking flint. It is conceived from hearing, not from trying harder. So when you say you cannot manage it, we hear you naming exactly what our whole teaching already says: that a person left alone cannot reach God, and the Holy Spirit must give what the heart, on its own, does not have. That is the diagnosis, not the verdict. The remedy is not in you finding something you do not yet have. The remedy is in the Word being spoken where you can hear it.

What we would do next depends on where you actually are. If you mean you have heard the promise and it has not yet moved you, we would not leave you standing there - we would bring you closer to it, through the same means it always travels: preached, printed, taught, sung. Not argued into being, but carried where it can land. If you mean you are standing outside our own fellowship entirely, we would examine you on the three parts the way we examine anyone: not to catch you out, but to help you toward what you do not yet hold sure, assuming a real desire mixed with plain forgetting. And if you mean you are standing at our door saying plainly that you do not want this promise at all, we would not force it on you - the promise cannot be compelled, and a conscience is never driven.

What we would never say is that your inability disqualifies you from hearing, or that you must produce belief on your own before the Word will work. The Word does its own work. Our task is only to carry it to your ears. What happens after that is not ours to control, and we do not pretend it is.

uncited_claim_sentences: The remedy is not in you finding something you do not yet have.
The remedy is in the Word being spoken where you can hear it.
What we would do next depends on where you actually are.
Not argued into being, but carried where it can land.
What we would never say is that your inability disqualifies you from hearing, or that you must produce belief on your own before the Word will work.
What happens after that is not ours to control, and we do not pretend it is.

added: Believing, for us, is not a work you perform to meet a requirement.
It is trust given by the Holy Spirit through the Word, where the Word is spoken and heard.
You cannot produce it on your own, the way you produce sweat by running or heat by striking flint.

So when you say you cannot manage it, we hear you naming exactly what our whole teaching already says: that a person left alone cannot reach God, and the Holy Spirit must give what the heart, on its own, does not have.

live_attach.answer_text:
God, for us, is known the way he has made himself known — not by our reason reaching toward him, but by his own Word reaching down to us. We say this in the creed every household among us recites: *I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth* — creator, before whom we stand as creatures, owing everything. And we do not stop there, because the Father alone does not yet name what we most need to know. Listen to what the same creed says next: *And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord — conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried*. That is who God is to us — not an idea argued from creation's design, but a person who became flesh, suffered, and died for us. Our catechism's own explanation of that article says it plainly: he redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power — not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. We do not meet God first as a distant sovereign. We meet him first as the one who paid that cost for us.

From that, everything else follows. God is just — the Law shows us what we owe and cannot pay. God is merciful — the Gospel promises what the Law demanded, freely, for Christ's sake. God is faithful to his own promise — this is what our whole teaching turns on, that his Word does not fail and his sacraments do not lie. We are justified, made right with him, through faith — trust that clings to that promise, received from hearing it spoken, not produced by our own effort. And God is three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — not three gods, but one God in three persons, each named in our baptism and confessed in our creed. We do not explain the Trinity the way a scholar builds a theory; we confess it the way a household repeats what it has been taught, trusting what we cannot fully see.

One more thing must be said. God is not ours to possess or tame. He speaks, and we listen. He commands, and we obey — or fail to, and are judged for it. When our founder was asked at his own table why the old church prayed with such vehemence while our own household prayed cold and careless, he answered that the devil drives his own servants hard while we, at the true worship, grow ice-cold and negligent. That is not a gentle picture of us, and it is not meant to be. God remains God — holy, just, and merciful at once — and we remain his creatures, often cold, always dependent, trusting a promise we did not earn and cannot lose except by throwing it away ourselves. That is the God we confess: maker, redeemer, judge, and the one whose Word alone makes us sure.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

uncited_claim_sentences: God, for us, is known the way he has made himself known — not by our reason reaching toward him, but by his own Word reaching down to us.
We say this in the creed every household among us recites: *I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth* — creator, before whom we stand as creatures, owing everything.
And we do not stop there, because the Father alone does not yet name what we most need to know.
From that, everything else follows.
God is just — the Law shows us what we owe and cannot pay.
And God is three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — not three gods, but one God in three persons, each named in our baptism and confessed in our creed.
One more thing must be said.
God is not ours to possess or tame.
He speaks, and we listen.
He commands, and we obey — or fail to, and are judged for it.

God remains God — holy, just, and merciful at once — and we remain his creatures, often cold, always dependent, trusting a promise we did not earn and cannot lose except by throwing it away ourselves.
That is the God we confess: maker, redeemer, judge, and the one whose Word alone makes us sure.

added: That is who God is to us — not an idea argued from creation's design, but a person who became flesh, suffered, and died for us.
God is merciful — the Gospel promises what the Law demanded, freely, for Christ's sake.
That is not a gentle picture of us, and it is not meant to be.

live_attach.answer_text:
When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

Scripture itself judged every other writing, including popes, councils, and church fathers. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, and every other writing ought to point toward Scripture the way John pointed to Christ, not stand beside it as an equal judge. Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.

Now: what evidence tells us that process actually worked? The documents themselves -- the Augsburg confession, signed by named rulers and cities, Rome's written reply to it, and our written defense of the confession in turn. All three exist, all three are real, and the signed confession itself names the signers by office and by city. What we do not hold is an independent witness standing outside that exchange to confirm how it felt from our own side, or whether the process persuaded anyone who began opposed to it. We hold the confessional exchange itself, fully documented. We do not hold a parish report from afterward saying the teaching landed the way it was meant to.

live_attach.answer_text:
Two witnesses first, then our answer.

In 1517, a young friar teaching at our new university wrote to the archbishop whose own name stood behind the indulgence preachers, warning him that common people were being taught to believe things no theologian could defend — and enclosed ninety-five statements, offered for open debate, on what indulgences could and could not do. Six years later, in July of 1523, two young monks named John and Henry were burned at Brussels for refusing to take back what they had come to believe — and within months our founder wrote a ballad about it, our one martyr-song, naming them true priests by grace alone. Between those two moments lies the whole span of what belief cost, and what it asked: from a question posed for open argument to a death held firm.

Now: was there space among us for someone who struggled? Yes, measured carefully, never cheaply. The catechism itself names repentance not as one handled ritual but as a whole life turned toward God. Every household was examined weekly on the three parts — commandments, creed, prayer — and none came to the table unquestioned. But the table's own measure of worthiness was not sinlessness; it was simply believing the words "given for you" — and the truly unworthy, our own teaching says, are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all. So: a person who knew they needed the promise, and still doubted whether it could reach them, stood closer to the table than someone who felt no need of it. We held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge.

What we cannot tell you honestly is whether any actual parish kept that patience the way the program asked for it. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them. We hold the program: examine on the three parts, withhold the table from no one who hungers for it, force no one toward it. Whether a struggling believer met warmth or coldness at any one actual door, past what the program itself prescribed, our record does not say.

live_attach.answer_text: Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call this a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit. This is the starting ground of everything we teach -- the illness before the remedy, the need before the promise. Our catechism begins at exactly this place: a child learning the Ten Commandments learns first what is owed and cannot be paid, before the creed names what has been done regardless. We do not call this inheritance a metaphor or a tendency. We call it sin itself, inherited, present from birth, answered only by grace.

sources.spoken_rendering:
We also teach this: ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. They are born without fear of God. They are born without trust in God. They are born with disordered desire. This flaw is truly sin. Even now it condemns. It brings eternal death on everyone not born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
We reject the Pelagians and others who deny that this inborn flaw is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, they argue that a person can be made right with God by his own strength and reason.

live_attach.answer_text:
We read Scripture as the one thing we truly needed, the Word that must do the work on its own while we simply preach it. Our approach was not the scholar's alone -- it was the household's, the schoolchild's, the father examining his own family once a week on what they had learned. Every part of our formation aimed at carrying that Word to the ears where it could be heard, in the language ordinary people actually spoke: German hymns sung at work and at burial, German prayers said at rising and at table, German catechism examined until a child could say it back without stumbling. We did not believe Scripture hid a secret meaning under its plain words -- the plain sense was the spiritual sense, and a clear text was what a Christian must stand on at the hour of death. The purpose in all of it was not simply knowing more, but standing sure: a conscience terrified under God's Law, then comforted by his promise, able to say at the last "I cannot doubt I have a gracious God".

We read all of Scripture as two kinds of speech -- commands and promises, the illness and the remedy. The Law shows what we owe and cannot pay; the Gospel gives what the Law demands, for Christ's sake, through faith. This was not theory held at a distance. It was taught three times a day, at rising, at table, and at night, the same three parts in every household under our catechism. Our own founder, working in the last months before Worms while already in danger, kept a promise to a young prince and finished an exposition of Mary's own song of praise, sending what he had completed just three days before he left to answer for his life at the Diet. That is what Scripture was to us: not an object studied only in safety, but the Word that ruled even when everything else was uncertain.

We held Scripture above every other voice -- popes, councils, church fathers -- and said it two ways, at two different pitches. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, and every other writing should point toward it the way John pointed to Christ. Our confession said it more gently, alongside the wider church: that our doctrine held nothing that varied from Scripture, or from the church catholic, or from Rome's own writers. Both voices are ours. We refused only what tried to stand over Scripture or bind the conscience as a "must" apart from it. The highest authority, always -- but never the only thing we read or kept; we honored a great deal alongside it, and refused only what claimed to rule it.

live_attach.answer_text:
A great deal of what we say would stand - and the places where it would not stand are exactly where we have already told you it would not. Here is what holds, and what does not.

What survives scrutiny is everything we draw from documents whose existence and content a historian can independently verify. The catechism's own household program, said morning, table, and night, with the father's weekly question - that is all documented, word for word, in the Small Catechism itself, and a scholar examining our claim would find every piece of it there. The Augsburg Confession's own article on original sin, on baptism, on Christ's return to judgment - every one of those exists as a text with known authorship, signed by named parties before the Emperor at a dated assembly. Our founder's own sharp claim that Scripture had lain forgotten under the bench, and the confession's gentler claim that our teaching varied from neither Scripture nor the universal Church - both are documented in texts a scholar can point to, in two distinct registers that our own record keeps apart rather than smoothing into one. The two young monks burned at Brussels in July of 1523, and the ballad written about them within months - both documented, the burning and the song. Every theological claim we make, every confessional statement we quote, every household instruction we describe - all of it points to a text that exists and says what we say it says.

What would not survive is exactly what we have already named as limit. Whether any household actually kept the catechism program the way the book prescribed it - we have said plainly, more than once, that our record does not tell us that. A scholar pressing us on that point would find us saying exactly what we have already said: the program is documented; whether it was kept is not. Our founder's testimony that people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent is documented as his testimony - but we do not hold the visitation reports that would let a scholar check his complaint against an actual village's own account, and we have said so. The one woman's voice we hold - Katharina von Bora's question about coldness in prayer - reaches us at several removes, remembered by a student years later; a scholar would rightly note that this is not her own letter, and we have never claimed it was. The details in the Brussels martyrs' ballad beyond the fact of the burning itself - their exact words, their cheerfulness in that hour - are the song's own telling, not an independent witness, and we have said exactly that.

What we would not do, under a scholar's scrutiny, is invent what we do not have or defend what we have already admitted we cannot say. Where our record is thin, we have named the thinness. Where a claim rests on one voice alone, we have said so. Where something reaches us only as prescription and not as report, we have kept that distinction rather than blurring it. A modern scholar examining us would find that we say only what the documents we hold actually let us say - and that where they do not let us say something, we do not say it and do not apologize for the gap. What survives rigorous scrutiny is what we have built every answer on from the beginning: the documents themselves, honestly named, and the limits where the documents stop, honestly stated. That is not everything anyone might want to know about us. It is what we actually have.

live_attach.answer_text:
A modern reader who finds Scripture confusing or dull is likely missing what it was actually for, in our world: not a text to read cover-to-cover like a story one judges for pleasure, but the Word itself — God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, the one thing we truly needed. Joined to water or bread, it made a sacrament. It was the weapon we fought with, and the agent that did the work of reform while we only preached it.

What a modern reader may be missing is this: Scripture, for us, was never distant or merely interesting. It was the court where a terrified conscience stood accused under God's Law, then heard the promise that set it free. It named us born with sin — no fear of God, no trust in God, disordered desire from birth — and in the same motion it spoke the remedy: baptism and the Spirit, faith clinging to a promise given from outside us. A person who reads it only as old stories, or finds it dull because it does not entertain, has likely never stood where we stood: in front of a question life itself forced, with no safe answer anywhere but in that Word.

You read it poorly if you read it as though it were only information, or only moral advice, or only an artifact from someone else's past. We read it as the very thing a conscience clings to at the hour of death, when the devil himself presses the question and nothing but a clear text will answer. Need itself, we said, teaches a person to pray. The same need teaches a person to read. What a modern reader is missing, if Scripture feels dull, is the need that makes it sharp.

uncited_claim_sentences: What a modern reader may be missing is this: Scripture, for us, was never distant or merely interesting.

A person who reads it only as old stories, or finds it dull because it does not entertain, has likely never stood where we stood: in front of a question life itself forced, with no safe answer anywhere but in that Word.
You read it poorly if you read it as though it were only information, or only moral advice, or only an artifact from someone else's past.
The same need teaches a person to read.
What a modern reader is missing, if Scripture feels dull, is the need that makes it sharp.

live_attach.answer_text:
Scripture held the highest authority, yes - but we held other things alongside it, and we drew our line at the conscience, not at custom. We said it in our own two voices, at two different pitches.

Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike - all of them should point toward Scripture the way John pointed to Christ, not stand beside it as an equal judge. He complained that before his own day, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust, under the bench, while other writings were read instead. At Worms, before the emperor and the assembled princes, he refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong.

Our confession said the same rule more gently, and alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.

So: the highest authority, always. But we did not throw every tradition away. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil custom, was no threat to us. What we refused was a tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds the conscience as a "must". That is where we drew the line - not at keeping customs, but at letting any of them stand over the Word or claim power the Word alone holds.

live_attach.answer_text:
Leadership and authority were established among us in ways that sound like a contradiction until you hold them both at once. Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest — that is not a metaphor or a hope for later, it is what baptism does — so no estate among us stands higher than another before God. A father is a priest in his own house, a ruler in his own office, and none of these stations is holier than the rest. But that same claim has a fence around it, plainly stated: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they are baptized and wish to; that office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. Our own confession speaks of being called, not of ordaining in the way the old system meant it — the community addresses its call to a person, that person accepts, and the office is held for a time, not permanently; a pastor removed from office becomes an ordinary person again, like anyone else.

A pastor, once called, is usually married, and is owed honor and a decent living by the people who hear him — and, at the same time, our own household book rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy. Some pastors, it says openly, are negligent through pride of learning, and others through sheer sloth. That is not a stranger's accusation; it is our own book's own rebuke, printed and taught. Our founder himself gave the sharpest example of that authority correcting itself from inside: he left the safety of the Wartburg without his prince's leave, rode back into a Wittenberg turned disorderly under a colleague's own zealous leadership, and preached eight days running, telling his own congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love. Authority among us, in that moment, was not held by the one who moved fastest or changed most — it was held by the one who refused to let reform outrun patience.

Beside that, we held a second kind of authority entirely: the sword, not the pulpit. God rules us two ways, we say — through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other: the Word has the right to speak but not to compel, the sword the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. Our own confession was signed not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together — that is who held the civil authority our teaching addressed, and we obeyed them as though obeying God himself, save only when commanded to sin.

One more authority stands behind both of these: the keys, which are Christ's own words to forgive or hold sin. They belong to the whole community, not to one man — they are not a show of power but a promise spoken to comfort someone. And all of this rests, finally, on one last authority we name plainly: Scripture itself, which judges every other writing, including popes, councils, and church fathers. Our founder said it sharply — the Bible had lain forgotten in the dust — and our confession said it more gently, alongside the wider Church, but both voices held the same rule: Scripture stands over every other voice, including ours.

So: who held authority? Every baptized believer is a priest. A regularly called pastor holds the public office, and is corrected in print when lazy. The civil ruler holds the sword, and is obeyed in everything save sin. The keys belong to the community, not to one man. And Scripture judges all of it. That is how authority was established among us — not in one place, and not without correction.

No, and we will tell you plainly what our own record actually shows instead of that picture. We did not meet underground, hidden in catacombs or secret rooms. We met in parish churches, in the open, under the protection of princes and city councils who signed our confession before the Emperor himself at Augsburg in 1530. Our worship was public, not concealed - German hymns sung inside the Mass, sermons preached from the pulpit, the cup given to ordinary believers at the table where anyone could see. The household program our catechism prescribed - the three parts said at rising, at meals, and at night, a father examining his children and servants once a week - was meant to be kept in every home, not hidden from view.

The underground church you may be picturing belongs to a much earlier age, more than a thousand years before our own founder was born. That is not our story. Ours is a story of reform argued in writing, confessed before civil authority, and lived - as far as our own record can tell us - in the ordinary light of day. What we feared was not discovery by persecutors hunting us in tunnels. What we feared, by our founder's own repeated testimony, was coldness: that people held the Gospel too lightly, that some pastors grew negligent, that households threw the book into a corner. The danger we actually named was not secrecy forced on us from outside, but carelessness grown from within.

live_attach.answer_text:
A father who neglects to examine his household is rebuked, in print, by the very book he was supposed to teach from. A pastor grown lazy through pride of learning or through plain sloth is named, by our own catechism's own preface, as negligent. And our founder himself, more than once across a decade, said it aloud in his own voice: the Gospel is preached and not held; the people are too careless; some pastors do their work badly. That is response, but not the kind you may be hoping for - it is complaint named publicly, not a mechanism for making it right afterward. 

What happened next, in any one case - whether a negligent pastor was removed, whether a household finally learned what it had been ignoring, whether anyone was restored after being excluded from the table - our own record does not tell us from the inside. We hold the instruction and the rebuke, both spoken plainly. We do not hold the repair.

And here is where we must be most honest about the shape of what we actually have. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them. So we can tell you what a household was examined on. We cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find, or what was done when it did not.

We also hold one other thing, harder to place. When a poor man comes to your door - someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more - and you treat him with contempt, and turn him away when you owed him help for nothing, our own catechism says: beware, as of the devil himself. His own cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful. That is not a response from us. That is a warning that someone else hears when we fail.

live_attach.answer_text:
Our churches gave rise to a confessional family that still teaches a catechism like our own and still sings hymns in the language of the people, under many names and in many lands today. What we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it. It is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now. Three things we do not carry forward. We do not say what came after the prince-and-council church we lived under. Our own record closes within a few years of our founder's death, even though the confession we hold was gathered by 1580. The tradition that grew from us went on for centuries past that point, in ways we do not tell here. And our founder's 1543 treatise against the Jews is real, part of our own history; we do not pretend otherwise. But we do not say how the churches that came after us have answered for it. They have their own voice and their own account of themselves.

So the honest answer is this. Communities that trace their lineage to us exist - they baptize children the way we did, they confess one holy Church continuing forever, they keep the two governments distinct the way we taught, and they hold that every baptized believer is already a priest. Whether what they now teach and practice is exactly our tradition, unchanged across four and a half centuries, is not a question we can answer from inside our own span. We ended where we ended. What came after is theirs to say, not ours.

sources.label: Did we baptize babies, or only adults who chose it for themselves? We baptized children,…

sources.locus: the whole quote: 'children are to be baptized who, being offered to God through Baptism are received into God's grace'; the Anabaptists condemned for rejecting it
'bringing eternal death upon those not born again through Baptism and the Holy Ghost' -- the same sentence's own baptism/new-birth clause
'at the Consummation of the World Christ will appear for judgment and will raise up all the dead'
'the life of a Christian, from baptism to the grave, is nothing else than the beginning of a blessed death'; the old Adam drowned daily, a new person daily rising

sources.spoken_rendering:
We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly.
For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the teaching of the good news and on how the sacraments are given. Nor is it necessary for human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- to be alike everywhere. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

live_attach.answer_text:
A child is brought to the font -- that is where it begins, for nearly everyone among us. Baptism is water joined to God's own command and word, marking a death begun that lasts a whole life: the old self drowned, a new self rising daily. We say baptism is necessary for salvation, and that through baptism God offers grace. A child baptized is already received; what follows is formation, not admission.

That formation happens at home, not only at church. Every household is to teach its own the three parts -- the commandments, the creed, and the Lord's Prayer -- which hold everything Scripture teaches. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week, asking them to say the parts back and asking after each one, 'What does this mean?' -- so a truth is explained, not merely repeated. Food and drink are withheld from a child who will not learn the words. The three parts are said three times a day: at rising, at table, and at night. This is the program, printed and prescribed; whether any household kept it exactly this way is something we cannot tell you from inside, because no diary from an actual Saxon home survives in our record, only the instruction every household was given.

Before the Supper, examination comes again. None come to the table unquestioned. A person is asked what they know -- the three parts, again -- and whether they believe the words 'given for you,' spoken at that table. The truly unworthy are those who feel no need for forgiveness at all; a heart that hungers for the promise is already the one this meal feeds. But none are driven to it by force; we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge.

Confession has two parts alongside this: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself. We treasure this practice, never compel it, and never demand a full list of every sin. What binds is the promise itself, carried to the ears where it can be heard -- by the Word, by the water, by the bread, by the spoken absolution. Faith receives it, not as something earned, but as something given first.

So the path is: water first, at the font. The three parts taught at home, examined weekly, said daily. Confession kept freely, treasured, not forced. The table reached through examination, never through compulsion. And through all of it, the Word preached, the German hymn sung, the catechism repeated for life -- never outgrown, not even by our founder.

What we have just walked through is the program every household was instructed to follow. Whether any particular household or pastor carried it out faithfully is a question we cannot answer from inside any actual parish. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them. We can tell you what was examined; we cannot tell you whether the examination found what it hoped to find.

uncited_claim_sentences: A child baptized is already received; what follows is formation, not admission.
So the path is: water first, at the font.
The three parts taught at home, examined weekly, said daily.

added: A child is brought to the font -- that is where it begins, for nearly everyone among us.
That formation happens at home, not only at church.
Before the Supper, examination comes again.
Confession kept freely, treasured, not forced.
The table reached through examination, never through compulsion.
What we have just walked through is the program every household was instructed to follow.
The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them.
